earlier_scan.source_named: Glottolog bata1295 lists only wordlists/surveys (Cowan 1953, Gravelle 1978, Arnold 2020 'Four undocumented languages of Raja Ampat'); no phonology or grammar of Batanta exists

new_statements.quote: Unlike Maˈya, there is no contrastive lexical stress in Batta; with a handful of exceptions, stress is predictably word‑final. As introduced above, a large proportion of the polysyllabic lexicon of Batta (approximately two thirds) can be analysed as sesquisyllabic, in that the nucleus of non‑final syllables is an underspecified vowel (represented here as /ə/), the realisation of which is determined by a combination of the vowel of the final syllable and the surrounding consonants. [p. 27:] In the onset of stressed (i.e., word-final) syllables, possible realisations of /q/ are [q], fricative [χ], or pharyngeal stop [ʡ]; in the onset of unstressed (i.e., non-final) syllables, /q/ may be realised as [q], [χ], or [ʡ], or be deleted

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Batta is not contrastive and falls predictably on the word-final syllable (which is also the only syllable that may carry one of the three lexical tones High/Rise/Low); non-final syllables are unstressed and mostly have a reduced/underspecified vowel (sesquisyllabic words).
new_statements.exceptions: 'with a handful of exceptions' (not itemised in the sketch). Toneless words optionally take a prepausal epenthetic /-o/; the sketch does not say whether this epenthetic syllable affects stress. Arnold 2025 (OL, accepted ms p. 41) corroborates: 'today all Salawati-Batta varieties have predictable final stress'; ms p. 36 and Table 25: Batta has no contrastive stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement (lexical/phonological word incl. subject prefixes); based on survey data (429-item list plus elicitation, 2019 and 2023, Yenenas village). Batta is a tone language (High, Rise, Low vs toneless, culminative but not obligatory, restricted to the final syllable) with an explicit stress statement.
new_statements.identity_note: The source calls the language 'Batta' (Glottolog bata1295 'Batanta', alt. name 'Batta'; Arnold's CV explicitly tags Batta as [bata1295]). Described variety: Batta of Yenenas village (also spoken in Weyman and Wailebet), south coast of Batanta island; c. 150 speakers, all born before c. 1980. Arnold treats Batta as a distinct language closely related to (possibly a divergent dialect of) the Salawati varieties (made1253), within Ma'ya-Salawati. Glottolog 5.1 still lists Batanta as undocumented/possibly extinct with zero descriptive refs; Arnold 2026 (LD&C 20) is the first published sketch and supersedes the earlier scan verdict 'NO-SOURCE-FOUND'.

sources.note: Sec. 3.1 (pp. 27-30): 'Unlike Ma'ya, there is no contrastive lexical stress in Batta; with a handful of exceptions, stress is predictably word-final' (p. 28); p. 27 glosses stressed = word-final, unstressed = non-final syllables. Batta has three lexical tones (High, Rise, Low) plus toneless, tone almost always on the final syllable; sesquisyllabic profile.
